Photograph: Guy Corbishley/AlamyView image in fullscreenHousing starts in London rose by 298% year on year in the 12 months to the end of June, although the number of homes completed was only 9% higher, at 18,050. Photograph: Guy Corbishley/AlamyConstruction industry‘It’s in quite a dark place’: why UK housebuilding is strugglingThe sector is in retreat across parts of the county, with developments paused. Despite a grim outlook for 2027 there is some cause for hope

Phillip InmanThu 26 Nov 2026 07.00 GMTLast modified on Thu 26 Nov 2026 09.28 GMTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA shopping centre in London that was due to be knocked down and replaced with a retail emporium and more than 1,000 apartments has been paused, dealing another blow to the government’s housing targets.

Lewisham council’s Green administration, which swept into power in May, insisted a larger number of affordable homes should be included in plans agreed last year with Labour officials.

Landsec, which owns the 1980s red-brick shopping centre in the borough’s town centre, said last month that the council’s demand, combined with “exceptionally challenging economic conditions”, had forced a rethink.

For London’s mayor, Sadiq Khan, the lack of progress in the capital’s south-east corner raises alarm bells as he tries to lift homebuilding across the city.

According to Damien Sharkey, the managing director of Hub, a mid-sized UK urban property developer with much of its work in London, the outlook for 2027 is “one of the most challenging in the firm’s 15-year history”.

After a collapse in housing starts to just 4,100 across London in 2025, figures have improved, with 16,290 homes registered in the year to the end of June 2026.

However, this impressive 298% year-on-year growth spurt only takes the capital back to where it was in 2023-24, and well below the 21,660 starts in 2022-23.

Khan’s efforts are not helped by a building safety levy on developers, expected to raise £3.4bn over 10 years, combined with extra regulations governing how to build and insulate tower blocks after the 2017 Grenfell Tower disaster.

View image in fullscreenA construction site in central London. Housebuilding in London’s private housing sector has fallen by 84% since 2015. Photograph: Ceri Breeze/AlamyThe consultants Molior has calculated that housebuilding in London’s private housing sector has fallen by 84% since 2015, despite the capital needing 88,000 new homes annually.

Housebuilding has also been in retreat in some other parts of the country – in the West Midlands, completions fell 7% in the year to June, while in north-west England they were 4% lower.

On Wednesday, the property and land development group Henry Boot said its performance this year would be “significantly below current market expectations”. Shares in the company, which builds homes mainly in the north of England,plunged by 20% to a 13-year low as it predicted it would make an underlying loss of up to £10m this year, blaming weak consumer and business confidence.

“In theory, Yorkshire-based property and land developer and housebuilder Henry Boot should be a beneficiary of Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s growth and levelling-up agendas, but the shares are getting flattened after a third profit warning this year,” says Russ Mould, the investment director at the platform AJ Bell.

“A weak housing market means housebuilders are cutting their purchases of land and Henry Boot, like Crest Nicholson earlier in the week, is also warning of both weak demand at its housebuilding business and the need to review the value of the land bank on its balance sheet,” Mould added.

View image in fullscreenCrest Nicholson is among housebuilders to warn of weak demand and need to review the value of its land bank. Photograph: Andrew Matthews/PAFigures from the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) show a decline in “new-build dwelling completions” in England from almost 43,000 in the second quarter of 2024 to below 36,000 in the same period this year. Annually, completions fell from about 212,000 in 2022-23 to 190,000 in 2024-25.

The weak housing market will dent the housing secretary Angela Rayner’s target of building 1.5m homes during this parliament, Most analysts believe is it is going to be about 500,000 short by the deadline in 2029.

Glenigan, a construction sector data provider, that charts the rise and fall of developments worth under £100m, says the outlook is grim after a steep decrease in the number of private-sector housing starts in the last year.

Allan Willen, the chief economist at Glenigan, says the private construction sector as a whole, including housing, infrastructure and commercial office building, has suffered over the last year.

“Build costs are high, lending has tightened and demand has softened in some sectors. As a result, numerous projects have been redesigned, delayed or cancelled.”

Those tough conditions are driving more building firms to the wall. About 3,800 firms in the construction sector went into insolvency in the last 12 months, more than any other UK industry sector.

While construction activity makes up only 6% of the economy, a decline in the wider property industry can have a devastating effect on the UK’s growth prospects. According to the latest quarterly figures, the building industry contracted by 0.7% in the three months to the end of September, holding back a rebound in the broader economy that still managed to expand by 0.7%.

Officially, the government’s 1.5m target is still in place, but a succession of profit warnings from big construction groups shows a difficult 2026 for the private sector, which is relied on for 60% of new-build home buildings, will continue next year.

The share price of Britain’s largest housebuilder, Barratt Redrow, has slumped from above 500p for much of 2024 to just 317p this week. Persimmon also suffered a drop in value after the US-Israel war on Iran began in February, followed by a slow recovery that still stops well short of values seen last year.

Reporting an annual loss of between £30m and £40m over the last year, Crest Nicholson has said this week it is struggling with a combination of costly remedial work on some sites and a slump in margins on new ones.

Meanwhile, Taylor Wimpey has cut its profit forecasts and said an industry-wide sales slowdown is in full swing and would “persist well into next year”.

Emily Williams, the director of residential research at the estate agents Savills, says a big issue facing housebuilders is a decline in prices, which she predicts will fall on average by 1.5% next year after zero growth in 2026.

Policymakers at the Bank of England are expected to pour more cold water on property prices next month with a rise in interest rates to 4.25%. There is the prospect of another by March next year.

Lower prices make homes more affordable, yet if the cost of borrowing is climbing and values falling, buying can seem more risky, putting off many purchasers. Rents, which are also affected by landlords’ higher borrowing costs, are on course to soar for the rest of the decade, putting many flats out of the reach of average earners.

Kelly Boorman, a property specialist at the accountants RSM, says popular myths about why developments are held up include planning constraints and a lack of land. Instead, she says the pressure comes from trying to calibrate what to build for a nervous audience.

“It’s quite a dark place for the housebuilders at the moment,” she says.

When Labour was elected in 2024, the outlook seemed very different. The property industry was ready to cast the pandemic into history and gear up for a boom.

An overhaul of planning laws and a settled political landscape after many years of ministerial changes under the previous Tory administration gave the industry encouragement. However, a first budget that raised employment taxes – and then the Iran war – sucked all the air out of the celebratory mood.

Simon Rubinsohn, the chief economist at the Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors (Rics), says average price falls disguise some bright spots around the country.

He says house prices in the north-west and north-east of England, and Scotland are likely to prove resilient, while “those parts of the country where price falls are slightly more pronounced than the UK-wide average [in 2026] are expected to see some further softening through 2027”.

Willen says there is a glimmer of hope coming from the public sector, which he expects to stage a modest recovery in 2027 as councils and housing associations ramp up expenditure.

View image in fullscreenA Taylor Wimpey housing development. In contrast a modest recovery is predicted in the public sector housebuilding. Photograph: Eddie Keogh/ReutersOne avenue will be to buy up homes left unsold by private developers. Or, at an earlier stage, commit to buying homes for rent as part of a new development package deal. This move will free up working capital for private sector firms wanting to invest in new schemes.

Sharkey explains: “We are seeing more local authorities able to buy up affordable homes from developers, which is needed at the moment.”

Hub operates in Leeds, Edinburgh and Bath, though mainly in London and south-east England. It has just completed a 270-home project in west London at White City, partnering with the charity Women’s Pioneer Housing (WPH), which owned the land. The project included a headquarters for WPH and 60 flats for rent that the charity controls, offering them to vulnerable women.

It is the type of scheme that Khan is keen to support, knowing that big developers such as Taylor Wimpey are stuck, trying to sell expensive flats with few buyers.
